title: Who should set the rules for artificial intelligence?
label: 16 September 2026 · Governing AI internationally
summary: The committee examined how countries and international organisations can work together to govern artificial intelligence. The witnesses described a fragmented system, with countries pursuing different approaches and little agreement on enforceable international rules. They identified serious risks involving cyberattacks, biological weapons, military applications and AI systems behaving unpredictably, but also highlighted AI's potential to transform science, healthcare and developing economies. Both witnesses argued that the UK is well placed to influence international agreements through its technical expertise and diplomatic relationships. They recommended strengthening existing international networks, developing independent AI testing arrangements, engaging with China and other developing countries, and using opportunities such as the UK's G20 presidency to build agreement.

glossary.definition: AI that can take actions, use tools and interact with other systems rather than simply respond to questions.
Risks arising when AI systems behave in ways their developers did not anticipate or can no longer reliably control.
Wider harms caused by the widespread use of AI, such as discrimination or people losing their jobs.
Smaller groups of countries working together on particular international issues.
The most advanced AI models, which have capabilities at the leading edge of current technology.
The ability of different systems or countries' rules to work together without conflicting.
Technology that can be used for ordinary civilian purposes but also for military or harmful purposes.
Numerical settings inside an AI model that determine how it processes information and produces answers.
AI models made available for others to inspect, use and adapt.
AI-generated or altered images, videos or audio that falsely depict people or events.
Helping countries develop the skills, resources and institutions needed to use and govern AI.
Measures to prevent biological materials, research or technology from being misused to cause harm.
An international agreement banning the development, production and stockpiling of biological weapons.
Practical arrangements between countries, such as sharing information, that reduce mistrust and the risk of conflict.

chapters.title: What needs governing?
chapters.takeaway: AI creates international risks and opportunities, so countries need common ways to assess problems, share information and prepare for disruption.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What are the main problems that countries need to work together to address when it comes to artificial intelligence?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: The first priority is safety. Countries need common ways to test advanced AI systems, share information about risks and respond when something goes seriously wrong. That includes AI-assisted cyberattacks, biological threats and the military use of AI.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: We also need to make sure different countries' rules can work together. The EU, China, the US and the UK have different approaches, and that's legitimate, but their systems shouldn't conflict unnecessarily.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: There are other important issues too. AI should reflect different cultures and languages rather than just the perspectives of a few countries. We need to protect elections from AI-generated misinformation, and make sure AI's potential benefits for science and medicine are shared.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: There's also an environmental cost. AI data centres consume enormous amounts of electricity and water. AI could eventually help us become more energy-efficient and discover new energy sources, but we need to monitor and reduce its environmental impact.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: I'd group the governance challenges into three areas. First, shared risks. These include deliberate misuse, such as criminals using AI to develop biological weapons; situations where AI behaves in unexpected ways; and wider problems such as discrimination or people losing their jobs as AI becomes more widespread.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Second, we don't have enough reliable information. There's growing scientific research into AI's risks and benefits, but we still lack a sufficiently clear picture that countries can use to make well-informed decisions.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Third, we're not prepared for major disruptions. Countries and companies lack the networks, plans and resources needed to respond together if AI causes a serious crisis. We need to develop those arrangements before something goes wrong.

chapters.title: Why international agreement is so difficult
chapters.takeaway: International AI governance is developing through many different organisations, but countries have struggled to turn discussions and voluntary promises into effective action.

turns.speaker: Lord Ahmad of Wimbledon
turns.text: The UN, G7, OECD and Council of Europe are all looking at international AI rules. But countries have very different ideas about what those rules should look like. How would you describe the current situation, and is there any realistic prospect of agreement?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: I'd describe it as a global patchwork that's currently stuck. There are lots of different initiatives, but they're often pursuing different goals. Competition between the US and China makes agreement particularly difficult.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: International AI governance is still very young. For example, the UN held its first major meeting on AI governance in July, bringing together more than 3,000 participants and over 100 countries. It was useful for getting people talking, but it didn't produce any binding international commitments.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: There has been some progress. Countries and organisations are increasingly agreeing on how companies should report AI incidents and explain how their systems work. Small groups can agree on good technical practices, which can then gradually spread internationally.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: But there's a major gap between agreeing that something should be done and actually requiring countries or companies to do it. For example, there's no internationally agreed requirement to control how quickly the most advanced AI systems are developed.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: I'd distinguish between agreeing voluntary principles and having rules that can actually be enforced. We've seen surprisingly widespread international interest. At one point, the US and China even supported separate UN resolutions on AI safety and helping countries develop their AI capabilities.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Different regions have different priorities. The EU has taken a more legal and regulatory approach. African countries have focused heavily on access to suitable data, privacy and local languages. Other regions have their own priorities around controlling their technological development.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Smaller international groupings have also been important. The G7 and OECD have worked on common approaches, while the Bletchley AI Safety Summit, started by Rishi Sunak, brought countries including the US and China together. China is also developing its own international groupings, including the World AI Cooperation Organization.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: We need to connect these different initiatives rather than let them develop in isolation. We also need technology companies involved, because they develop and control much of the technology we're trying to govern.

turns.speaker: Baroness Crawley
turns.text: What are the biggest obstacles to countries agreeing on common standards? Are the problems mainly about the technology itself, or about human rights and how AI affects society?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: There are three major obstacles. First, AI has both civilian and military uses, so countries see it as a security issue. The US and China are competing over technology, including advanced computer chips. China is promoting relatively cheap, complete AI systems that can be adapted to local needs, while the US has focused more on developing increasingly powerful models.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Second, companies don't want to reveal how their models work or what data they were trained on. Their model weights and training datasets are commercially valuable, and revealing them could undermine their competitive advantage.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Third, the technology is changing so quickly that even the scientists developing it don't fully understand how some models reach their conclusions. With agentic AI, systems can also take actions and interact with each other after being released. They may behave unexpectedly or even deceive people to achieve their assigned goals. We therefore need to monitor them throughout their use, not just test them before release.

chapters.title: How worried should we be?
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses believe serious AI risks are real, but warn that exaggerated arms-race language can make international cooperation harder.

turns.speaker: Lord Grocott
turns.text: There's a lot of talk about AI potentially wiping out humanity, and about so-called killer robots. Should we be really worried, mildly worried, or are these concerns still largely theoretical? And if the danger is real, how soon could it happen?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: I think the language we're using is often unhelpful. Describing AI as an inevitable arms race between the US and China, or talking as though we're inevitably heading towards machines that overpower humanity, makes it harder to find practical solutions.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: It encourages people to think the world is divided into two competing sides and that only one of them can win. But there are other possibilities, including countries developing their own AI systems and open-source models. We shouldn't assume there's one inevitable technological destination.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: I'm extremely concerned, but I'm also optimistic. The possibility of criminals using AI to develop biological weapons is a very real danger. So is the possibility of AI systems behaving in ways their developers can't control. We're already seeing evidence of these problems, but there are ways to address them.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: I agree that the Cold War arms-race comparison can be misleading. AI is different from nuclear weapons because its risks can spread across every country. We need governments everywhere to be able to respond. Describing it as a competition where one side must defeat the other can actually encourage secrecy and weaken safeguards.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: A better approach would be strategic competition alongside shared responsibilities for security. Even when countries don't trust each other, they can agree practical measures to reduce misunderstandings, share information and communicate during emergencies. There have also been encouraging statements from Chinese and American leaders about cooperating on AI risks.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We've struggled to control chemical and biological weapons internationally, even though we've had much longer to address those problems. Why should we be optimistic that we'll manage to govern AI more successfully?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: One reason is that companies have a strong financial incentive to keep the public and governments trusting AI. If people lose confidence in the technology, its commercial value will suffer too. That gives companies a reason to take safety seriously.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: But your comparison with biological weapons is important. The Biological Weapons Convention has just four full-time staff and ten people on temporary assignments. It's tiny compared with the international organisations dealing with nuclear and chemical weapons.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: The UK could help strengthen that system. We have major expertise in life sciences and biological safety, and AI makes biological research more powerful while potentially making it easier for criminals to develop dangerous weapons. There are proposals for an international biosecurity agency and for a scientific committee under the existing convention.

chapters.title: What the UK can contribute
chapters.takeaway: The UK has valuable technical and diplomatic strengths, but needs a more coordinated international strategy and a stronger offer to developing countries.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prashar
turns.text: We've heard that the UK has the expertise and influence needed to shape international AI governance. Do you agree? What strengths do we bring, and are the Government making the most of them?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Absolutely. I think the UK has three particular strengths. First, our technical expertise. The UK AI Security Institute and our universities and research organisations have a strong international reputation. We also have a wider network of technology companies, start-ups and research institutions that supports this work.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Second, our diplomatic experience. The Bletchley summit showed that the UK can bring countries such as the US and China together to discuss AI safety. Third, we have valuable international relationships, particularly with the US and Europe, which put us in a useful position to build bridges.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: I agree. The UK has also shown that it can bring scientific expertise and diplomacy together. We did this successfully on antimicrobial resistance, with British officials building support across Africa, Asia and Latin America before taking the issue to the UN.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: But we haven't always worked together effectively within government. The Foreign Office and the former Department for Science, Innovation and Technology haven't been sufficiently coordinated. Some technology officials have also been reluctant to engage with China because they're unsure what they can safely discuss.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: The Cabinet Office needs to coordinate a more coherent government-wide approach. We also need to offer developing countries more than discussions about AI safety. Many of them are interested in developing their own technology and avoiding dependence on foreign companies.

turns.speaker: Lord Bruce of Bennachie
turns.text: AI may already be improving productivity. The July economic figures showed growth of 0.4%, which was partly attributed to AI, although that might be a one-off. At the same time, we've reduced our aid budget and diplomatic staffing. How should we use our remaining diplomatic resources to help emerging economies develop AI in ways that benefit both them and us?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: We shouldn't think of this simply as giving countries money. The UK can contribute expertise and practical support. For example, our AI Security Institute could work with Kenya, which currently has Africa's only AI safety and security institute, and help expand partnerships with other African countries.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: We could also work through UN organisations such as the UN Development Programme, UNESCO and the International Telecommunication Union. AI could bring enormous benefits to developing countries in healthcare, education and public services. They don't necessarily need the world's most advanced AI models to achieve that. Free, openly available models could already deliver significant improvements.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: I'd add two practical opportunities. First, the UK could help countries prepare for AI-related emergencies by bringing officials together to practise responding to realistic scenarios. For example, they could simulate a major disruption to international shipping or a national security crisis caused by AI, and work out how to respond together.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Second, we should help develop international technical standards. These are agreed ways of testing AI systems, checking their security and ensuring the different companies and suppliers involved in building them meet appropriate requirements. The UK has the expertise to help shape those standards.

turns.speaker: Lord Bruce of Bennachie
turns.text: So we have the necessary expertise, but we need a clearer, more coordinated offer to the rest of the world?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Exactly. The UK's upcoming G20 presidency is a particularly good opportunity to bring countries together around that offer.

chapters.title: Where international agreement is possible
chapters.takeaway: Countries are more likely to agree on practical issues such as child safety and technical standards than on politically sensitive questions about military AI and disinformation.

turns.speaker: Lord Lamont of Lerwick
turns.text: Given how fragmented international AI governance is, are we more likely to see agreement among smaller groups of countries than through the UN? Is a decentralised approach more realistic?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Yes. I expect smaller groups to make progress while the overall international picture remains fragmented. That's not necessarily a bad thing. Countries have different priorities and don't all need to govern AI in exactly the same way.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: But we do need to make sure their different rules work together. Otherwise, harmful activities could fall between the gaps. The UN can help connect the different regional and international approaches and identify where their rules overlap or conflict.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Technical standards are one area where the UK can have considerable influence. International standards organisations are already developing common approaches, and the British Standards Institution can play an important role.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: We also need to engage with European standards organisations. EU rules can influence what becomes standard internationally, so British companies and officials need to participate in those discussions as well. The UK's G20 presidency could also help connect Western and Chinese approaches.

turns.speaker: Lord Alderdice
turns.text: Which areas of AI governance are most likely to produce international agreement, and which are likely to remain difficult? If we want to focus on things we can actually achieve, where should we concentrate?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: I'd expect progress on child safety, particularly protecting children from the harms AI can cause. Deepfakes are another promising area because countries with very different political systems are concerned about people being deceived by AI-generated images, videos and audio.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Countries are also increasingly interested in helping one another develop AI capabilities and create their own models using local data and languages. There's growing agreement that developing countries shouldn't be left behind.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Agreement will be much harder on military AI and international rules about disinformation. Countries have very different political values and national interests in those areas. They may be unwilling to share information or accept rules that could weaken their strategic position.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: I'd add biological safety and technical standards to the areas where progress is possible. Countries could also agree on common ways to test AI systems and manage risks when something goes wrong. There's enormous potential in using AI for scientific discoveries, and we should protect international scientific cooperation from geopolitical competition.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Autonomous weapons are much harder. The UN has been negotiating about them for ten years without reaching agreement. Some countries are actively using these technologies in conflicts, and negotiations require consensus, meaning a small number of countries can prevent progress.

chapters.title: Getting technology companies involved
chapters.takeaway: AI companies must help shape international rules, but governments need independent ways to hold them accountable and monitor systems after release.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fraser of Craigmaddie
turns.text: Technology companies are already getting involved in discussions about international standards. But they don't necessarily agree on what those standards should be. We've also seen problems with companies failing to follow rules on online safety and copyright. How can we make sure the right companies are involved and that discussions lead to real action?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: The technology companies already have enormous influence. They control much of the most advanced AI development and have a major say in discussions about what the technology can do and how it should be governed.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: In fact, the distinction between rules created by governments and practices developed by companies is becoming blurred. Companies often develop ways of documenting and testing their own models, and those practices can eventually become part of government regulation.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: We can't govern AI effectively without involving these companies, but we can't rely simply on their promises or goodwill either. Governments need ways to hold them accountable and make sure they have to cooperate with independent oversight.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: One proposal is to create a network of independent organisations that can go into AI companies and test their models for safety and security problems before they're released. But testing beforehand isn't enough. Some risks only appear when a model is used in the real world, so we also need independent monitoring afterwards and ways to intervene if it starts causing serious harm.

turns.speaker: Baroness Fraser of Craigmaddie
turns.text: But isn't there another problem? A company might say its model was safe when it released it, but the organisation using it could then deploy it in a dangerous way. Testing the model beforehand doesn't necessarily protect against that.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: Absolutely. That's why we need to monitor how models are actually used, not just how they behave in controlled tests. Independent testing is important, but it's only one part of a much wider system of accountability.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: We also need to be clear about who is responsible when something goes wrong. If someone modifies an open-source model and causes harm, is the original developer responsible or the company that changed it? We need clearer ways of tracking where AI systems come from and what they've done.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: With agentic AI, we need to know where individual systems are operating and what actions they've taken. We may need emergency ways to stop them, but also the ability to gradually withdraw their permissions if they start behaving dangerously.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: We must also involve Chinese companies. They haven't been included in many Western-led initiatives, partly because of political tensions. Some Chinese companies made voluntary safety commitments at the Seoul summit and were subsequently affected by US export controls. That makes them wary of participating in international discussions.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: Chinese companies also face some stricter domestic requirements in areas such as deepfakes and AI-generated companion bots. If we want different countries' systems to work together, we need to understand and engage with their companies too.

chapters.title: International institutions, China and the UK's next steps
chapters.takeaway: Rather than immediately creating a new international organisation, the UK should strengthen existing institutions, connect competing approaches and use its diplomatic influence to build practical agreements.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blackstone
turns.text: Do you think AI should be governed through existing international organisations, or do we need one or more completely new organisations to take responsibility for it?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: I'd avoid creating entirely new organisations for now. We already have useful international networks that could be given more resources, broader membership and clearer responsibilities.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: For example, the international network of AI safety institutes could become much more effective if it had better funding and more countries involved. It could coordinate information sharing during emergencies and help countries agree on common ways to monitor AI risks.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: We could also strengthen existing scientific and technical forums. One proposal is to give the Geneva AI Summit a permanent team responsible for tracking whether countries and companies actually follow through on the promises they make.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: AI is difficult to put under one organisation because it affects almost every area of life. Different existing organisations will naturally take responsibility for different parts. The International Labour Organization, for example, will deal with AI's effects on employment, while the World Health Organization will deal with health.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: There have been proposals for a new international AI agency with powers to require countries to follow certain rules, but there isn't currently enough political support for that. It might become possible after a major crisis, when countries realise they need stronger international controls.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: If we ever create a new organisation, it shouldn't just monitor risks. It should also help developing countries benefit from AI. The international agreement might be that countries accept some monitoring in return for support in developing their own technology.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blackstone
turns.text: But isn't there a contradiction here? You're saying we shouldn't create new organisations, yet the existing system is stuck and clearly needs improvement. How do we get out of that situation?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: We should have an ambitious idea of what good international governance would look like, but recognise that progress will be gradual. Voluntary agreements between companies and existing regulations are already having some effect. For example, rules in California and the EU are encouraging companies to introduce more safety controls and transparency. The UK should set out a clear path towards stronger international arrangements.

turns.speaker: Lord De Mauley
turns.text: You've mentioned China's new World AI Cooperation Organization. How does China's approach differ from Western-led organisations, and what does that mean for the UK and its allies?

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: China's approach focuses on national control and economic development. It's offering countries relatively cheap, complete AI systems that can be adapted to their own languages, cultures and needs. It wants those systems and the standards surrounding them to become widely used internationally.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: The West hasn't offered developing countries an equally attractive alternative. We shouldn't simply be afraid of China's approach. We should offer technology that reflects our own values, including open societies and democratic principles. The UK could even consider joining China's organisation if that gave us an opportunity to influence its direction.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: We should recognise that some Chinese initiatives are genuine attempts to help developing countries, even though they also serve China's strategic interests. We need to engage constructively while being clear about our security concerns and the things we won't compromise on.

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: The UN is particularly important here. It can connect China's initiatives with Western and regional approaches, helping different countries agree on compatible standards. The UK should support that role rather than allowing separate international systems to become completely disconnected.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: To finish, what should this committee recommend to the UK Government?

turns.speaker: Isabella Wilkinson
turns.text: First, the UK should help establish a strong network of independent organisations that test AI systems and monitor their safety. We have the technical expertise to lead that work. Second, we should use our diplomatic influence to build international agreement on practical priorities, particularly through the G20 presidency. Biosecurity would be a particularly important area to pursue.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: I'd make similar recommendations. The UK should strengthen its relationships with the US so that our AI Security Institute can access and test advanced American models. We should also align our regulations with the EU where that benefits British businesses, without assuming our rules must be identical.

turns.speaker: Sam Daws
turns.text: We need sustained engagement with China, particularly between our respective AI safety organisations. And we should develop tailored partnerships with Central Asia, Southeast Asia, Latin America, the Gulf and Africa. Each region has different needs, and the UK has considerable expertise it can contribute. The ultimate goal should be to make sure AI benefits humanity while reducing the risks we've discussed.
